bipartite.kami_theme: The cricket's cry on a frost-cold night, setting the scene of desolate autumn cold via sound and sensory perception of the mat itself
bipartite.shimo_theme: The speaker's resolve/resignation to lie down alone, spreading only his own robe, in solitude
bipartite.pivot_note: The kami-no-ku establishes the cricket's cry and the frost-cold night as sensory data (sound, cold) that the speaker experiences while lying on the narrow mat; the しき in さむしろに contains the pivot into 衣かたしき (spreading only one's own robe-sleeve), so the physical coldness and solitude perceived in the kami directly motivate and mirror the shimo's image of solitary sleep. The cricket's cry, traditionally imagined as calling to a mate, throws into relief the human speaker's forced solitude — the insect has its cry answered by nothing, as does the poet.

kakekotoba.interaction: さむしろ is itself a compound noun meaning 'narrow/small sleeping mat' but is heard simultaneously as containing 寒し 'cold', so the mat is presented as both a physical sleeping surface and an emblem of the cold night — the coldness of the frost-night (霜夜) bleeds into the texture of the mat on which the speaker must lie

kakekotoba.reading_primary: 片敷き (spreading only one layer/one side of one's robe)
kakekotoba.reading_secondary: 片敷き also evokes 難しき/難き nuance of hardship in some readings, though primary sense dominates
kakekotoba.interaction: The core meaning is spreading only one's own sleeve/robe as a solitary bed-mat instead of sharing two robes with a lover, directly expressing solitude; this is not a true double-grammar pivot but a conventional idiom for solitary sleep, included here for completeness though confidence is lower than the さむしろ pivot

kigo.note: The cricket (kirigirisu, an old term overlapping with what is now called koorogi) is a quintessential autumn insect in classical waka, its thin, plaintive cry conventionally signifying the approach of cold nights and the loneliness of autumn; paired with 霜夜 (frost-night) it reinforces late-autumn desolation and is the poem's dominant seasonal anchor, governing the emotional register of solitary longing that unfolds in the shimo-no-ku
